claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by inherently high dislocation mobility.
Low lattice friction facilitates the proposed high dislocation mobility.
Low effective stacking-fault energy facilitates the proposed high dislocation mobility and cross-slip.
High dislocation mobility promotes dynamic recovery during deformation.
Rapid cross-slip and dislocation annihilation prevent substantial dislocation accumulation.
Limited dislocation accumulation restricts strain hardening and thereby produces lower measured hardness and strength.
The applicable starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting solid solution is assumed to have a face-centered-cubic or similar lattice.
Changing strain rate and temperature will alter the balance between dislocation generation and dynamic recovery.
Higher strain rates will restrict dynamic recovery relative to room-temperature quasi-static deformation.
Lower testing temperatures will suppress dynamic recovery relative to room-temperature testing.
Suppressing dynamic recovery will increase stored dislocation density.
Increased dislocation storage will produce higher work-hardening rates, hardness, and strength.
Cold work followed by short annealing can tailor the initial dislocation structure so as to reduce immediate dynamic recovery.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi that remains a single-phase solid solution under the tested loading conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when additional phases or precipitates are present.
If dislocation density and mechanical properties do not increase significantly at higher strain rate or lower temperature, the dynamic-recovery hypothesis is falsified.

contradictions.description: The stated boundary is ambient to moderately low temperature, but the proposed falsification experiment includes 77 K, a cryogenic condition that is not ordinarily characterized as merely moderately low.
